statement: Kai's money box holds only 10-cent and 20-cent coins. There are 15 coins, worth 210 cents in total. How many 20-cent coins are there?

choices.misconception: I found that 210 is 60 more than 150, but then divided 60 by 20 instead of by 10.
I thought there would be about the same number of each coin, so I halved 15 and rounded up.
I worked it out correctly but gave the number of 10-cent coins instead of 20-cent coins.
I found how many 20-cent coins fit into 210 cents, 10 of them with 10 cents over, and forgot that there must be 15 coins in all.

hints: What if every coin were a 10-cent coin?
Start with all 15 coins as 10-cent coins and see how far short of 210 you are. Each swap to a 20-cent coin adds the same amount.
Fifteen 10-cent coins make 150 cents, which is 60 cents short. Each swap adds 10 cents.

solutions.reliable: If all 15 coins were 10-cent coins, they would make 150 cents. We need 60 cents more. Swapping one 10-cent coin for a 20-cent coin adds 10 cents, so we need $60 \div 10 = 6$ swaps: 6 coins of 20 cents and 9 of 10 cents. Check: $6 \times 20 + 9 \times 10 = 120 + 90 = 210$. The transferable idea: start from an easy guess and count how many swaps fix the total.
solutions.elegant: Back-solve from the choices: 6 coins of 20 cents and 9 of 10 cents make exactly 210 cents with 15 coins. Each other choice gives the wrong total.

whyOnTest: Two kinds of coins with a known count and total: the swap method is a classic way to solve it without algebra.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
